description: When a macro stores a module reference passed as an argument for use inside a generated function, expand the literal into that function's context with Macro.expand_literals/2 so it stays a runtime dependency instead of forcing recompilation.
title: Compile-time dependencies
body:
# ADR-001: Compile-time dependencies

## Context

Macros run at compile time, so using any macro adds a compile-time dependency from the calling module to the module that defines the macro. That dependency is expected and usually cheap.

The anti-pattern appears when the *arguments* passed to a macro also become compile-time dependencies. A macro that receives a module reference and embeds it into the module body (a module attribute, an `@before_compile` accumulator, anything outside a function clause) records that referenced module as a compile-time dependency of the caller, even when the referenced module is only invoked at runtime.

A compile-time dependency forces dependent recompilation: changing the referenced module, or any module in its transitive runtime dependency graph, forces the calling module to recompile. In a builder-style API (a request pipeline, a router, a plug stack) where many modules are registered through one macro, a single edit can fan out into a large recompilation graph and dominate incremental build time.

## Decision

### Rule 1: Expand module literals into the function context where they run

When a macro stores a module reference for use inside a generated function, expand the literal as if it already lived in that function with `Macro.expand_literals/2`, so the reference is recorded as a runtime dependency.

**Correct:**

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Pipeline do
  defmacro __using__(_opts) do
    quote do
      Module.register_attribute(__MODULE__, :stages, accumulate: true)
      @before_compile MyApp.Pipeline
    end
  end

  defmacro stage(mod) do
    mod = Macro.expand_literals(mod, %{__CALLER__ | function: {:call, 2}})

    quote do
      @stages unquote(mod)
    end
  end
end
```

**Wrong:**

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Pipeline do
  defmacro __using__(_opts) do
    quote do
      Module.register_attribute(__MODULE__, :stages, accumulate: true)
      @before_compile MyApp.Pipeline
    end
  end

  defmacro stage(mod) do
    quote do
      @stages unquote(mod)
    end
  end
end
```

A caller registers stages, and `@before_compile` reads `@stages` to emit a `call/2`:

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Web do
  use MyApp.Pipeline

  stage MyApp.Authentication
end

# generated by @before_compile:
def call(conn, _opts) do
  MyApp.Authentication.call(conn)
end
```

**Why:** In the wrong version, `stage MyApp.Authentication` runs at compile time and accumulates the module into the `@stages` attribute, outside any function body. That makes `MyApp.Authentication` a compile-time dependency of `MyApp.Web`, even though it is only ever called at runtime inside the generated `call/2`. Any change to `MyApp.Authentication`, or to its transitive runtime dependencies, then forces `MyApp.Web` to recompile. `Macro.expand_literals/2` resolves the literal as if it sat inside `call/2`, so the reference is tracked as a runtime dependency and edits to `MyApp.Authentication` no longer ripple back through the using modules. This holds only when the macro never calls a function on the module, accesses its structs, or reads its metadata at compile time. If it does any of those, the compile-time dependency is real and cannot be removed. To see which dependencies a file actually has, and whether each is compile-time, runtime, or export, run `mix xref trace path/to/file.ex`.

## Consequences

- Module references passed to macros are recorded as runtime dependencies instead of compile-time ones.
- Editing a referenced module no longer forces every using module, and its transitive graph, to recompile.
- Incremental compile times stay bounded as the number of registered modules grows.
- The technique applies only when the macro does not invoke functions, read structs, or inspect metadata of the module at compile time; when it must, the compile-time dependency is unavoidable.

description: When a macro's quote block contains substantial logic and is invoked many times, move the body into a regular function the macro calls so it compiles once instead of per call site.
title: Large code generation
body:
# ADR-002: Large code generation

## Context

A macro runs at compile time and injects its quoted AST into the calling module at every invocation site. The compiler then expands and compiles that injected code once per call site. When the quoted body is large and the macro is called many times, the cost multiplies: a web router with hundreds of `get/2` calls produces hundreds of independent copies of the macro body, each expanded and compiled into the host module's bytecode.

Two concrete costs follow. Compilation slows, because the compiler walks and compiles every copy of the generated code rather than one shared definition. The compiled artifact grows, because each expansion is duplicated into the `.beam` file; module size scales with the number of call sites times the size of the quoted body.

The fix is to keep the quoted body small. A macro only needs to generate code for the work that genuinely requires compile-time context (capturing `__MODULE__`, the literal arguments, or an attribute target). Everything else (validation, transformation, side effects) can run in an ordinary function the macro calls, so that logic is compiled once and dispatched to.

## Decision

### Rule 1: Quote a function call, not the function body

The macro's `quote` block should expand to a single call into a regular function, passing the unquoted arguments. Put the bulk of the work in that function.

**Correct:**

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Router do
  defmacro get(route, handler) do
    quote do
      MyApp.Router.__define__(__MODULE__, unquote(route), unquote(handler))
    end
  end

  def __define__(module, route, handler) do
    if not is_binary(route) do
      raise ArgumentError, "route must be a binary"
    end

    if not is_atom(handler) do
      raise ArgumentError, "handler must be a module"
    end

    Module.put_attribute(module, :store_route_for_compilation, {route, handler})
  end
end
```

**Wrong:**

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Router do
  defmacro get(route, handler) do
    quote do
      route = unquote(route)
      handler = unquote(handler)

      if not is_binary(route) do
        raise ArgumentError, "route must be a binary"
      end

      if not is_atom(handler) do
        raise ArgumentError, "handler must be a module"
      end

      @store_route_for_compilation {route, handler}
    end
  end
end
```

**Why:** In the wrong version the entire validation-and-store body is the quoted AST, so it is inlined into the host module at every `get/2` call. A router with hundreds of routes expands and compiles hundreds of full copies of that body; compilation time and the resulting `.beam` size grow with the call count. In the correct version the `quote` injects one small call. The validation and `Module.put_attribute/3` logic is compiled exactly once as `__define__/3`, and each call site costs a single fixed-size dispatch regardless of how much work the function does. The macro is still justified here because it needs compile-time context (`__MODULE__` and the literal route); if a construct needs none of that, it should be a plain function rather than a macro (see ADR-003).

## Consequences

- Each call site expands to a fixed-size function call, so macro expansion cost stays flat as the number of invocations grows.
- The bulk logic compiles once into one named function; host-module bytecode and `.beam` size no longer scale with call count.
- Compilation time scales with call sites times a small stub instead of call sites times the full body.
- The extracted function is callable and testable on its own, unlike logic buried in quoted AST.

description: When a defmacro only computes over its already-evaluated arguments, replace it with a named function to drop the require dependency and inline expansion.
title: Unnecessary macros
body:
# ADR-003: Unnecessary macros

## Context

A macro is meta-programming. Its arguments arrive as quoted AST at compile time, its return value is also AST, and that AST is spliced into the call site and compiled in place. A function is different: it receives already-evaluated values at runtime and runs as one shared compiled body. The two mechanisms are not interchangeable. A macro is the right tool only when the code must inspect or transform unevaluated code before it runs (deferred evaluation, AST inspection, generating definitions).

Reaching for `defmacro` where a plain function would do adds cost and removes capability for nothing. Every caller must `require` the defining module, which creates a compile-time dependency on it (ADR-001), and when that dependency goes untracked it silently goes stale (ADR-005). The macro body expands into each call site instead of living in one place, and the macro is not a runtime value, so it cannot be captured with `&`, passed as an argument, or piped. Because macros are harder to write, read, and reason about, indiscriminate use compromises maintainability while buying nothing in return.

## Decision

### Rule 1: Use a named function unless the code must manipulate unevaluated code

**Correct:**

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Math do
  def sum(a, b), do: a + b
end

MyApp.Math.sum(3, 5)
MyApp.Math.sum(3 + 1, 5 + 6)
```

**Wrong:**

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Math do
  defmacro sum(a, b) do
    quote do
      unquote(a) + unquote(b)
    end
  end
end

require MyApp.Math
MyApp.Math.sum(3, 5)
```

**Why:** The macro computes nothing the function cannot; both produce `8`. But `sum/2` as a macro runs at compile time on the AST of its arguments, forces every caller to `require MyApp.Math`, and expands `unquote(a) + unquote(b)` inline at each call site instead of sharing one compiled body. That `require` is a compile-time dependency (ADR-001). The function version drops the `require`, exists as a real runtime value (capturable as `&MyApp.Math.sum/2`, passable, pipeable), and is simpler to read, test, and reason about. Reserve `defmacro` for code that must operate on unevaluated AST.

## Consequences

- `defmacro` is reserved for code that must inspect or transform unevaluated AST, so its presence signals genuine meta-programming rather than an ordinary computation in disguise.
- The logic stays plain runtime code: directly testable in isolation and composable with the rest of the language, with no quoting, unquoting, or macro hygiene to get wrong.
- Readers and tooling reason about the call as data flow, not as an expansion they must perform in their heads.

description: When a library exposes a `__using__/1` that only imports or aliases other modules, replace `use` with explicit `import`/`alias` at the call site.
title: `use` instead of `import`
body:
# ADR-004: `use` instead of `import`

## Context

`import`, `alias`, and `use` all establish dependencies between modules, but `use` is categorically different. `import` and `alias` are lexically scoped directives: they shorten name resolution inside the file that writes them and generate no code. `use M, opts` instead expands at compile time to `require M; M.__using__(opts)`, and `__using__/1` is a macro whose returned quoted expression is spliced verbatim into the calling module.

Because that injected expression is arbitrary, it can import modules, alias modules, define functions, register attributes, and declare behaviours, all invisibly. The `use M` line at the call site reveals none of it. Reading it requires reading the internal details of `__using__/1` in `M`. This broad scope is the smell: an injected `import` silently shadows or conflicts with the caller's own functions, and a propagated `import` makes the caller compile-depend on a module it never named (the compile-time dependency machinery is ADR-001 and ADR-005). When the injected block grows large it compounds into ADR-002, and the question of whether the macro should exist at all is ADR-003.

## Decision

### Rule 1: Use `import`/`alias` when no code injection is needed

**Correct:**

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Library do
  def from_lib, do: "from library"
end

defmodule MyApp.Client do
  import MyApp.Library

  def foo, do: "local client function"

  def run, do: from_lib() <> " - " <> foo()
end
```

**Wrong:**

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Helpers do
  def foo, do: "from helpers"
end

defmodule MyApp.Library do
  defmacro __using__(_opts) do
    quote do
      import MyApp.Library
      import MyApp.Helpers   # propagates a dependency the caller never named
    end
  end

  def from_lib, do: "from library"
end

defmodule MyApp.Client do
  use MyApp.Library

  # ** (CompileError) imported MyApp.Helpers.foo/0 conflicts with local function
  def foo, do: "local client function"

  def run, do: from_lib() <> " - " <> foo()
end
```

**Why:** `use MyApp.Library` expands to `MyApp.Library.__using__([])`, and the macro's quoted body (two `import` directives) is spliced into `MyApp.Client`. Nothing at the `use` line states that `MyApp.Helpers` is now imported, so `foo/0` collides with the local definition and the module fails to compile. The caller also picks up a compile-time dependency on every propagated import (ADR-001, ADR-005). `import` and `alias` are lexically scoped: they only affect name resolution in the file that writes them and emit no code, so the dependency set and the available names are exactly what the directives list.

### Rule 2: When `use` is genuinely required, publish a nutrition facts label

**Correct:**

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Worker do
  @moduledoc """
  A supervised worker base.

  > #### `use MyApp.Worker` {: .info}
  >
  > When you `use MyApp.Worker`, it sets `@behaviour MyApp.Worker`
  > and defines a `child_spec/1` function so your module can be
  > started directly under a supervisor.
  """

  @callback handle_job(term()) :: :ok

  defmacro __using__(_opts) do
    quote do
      @behaviour MyApp.Worker

      def child_spec(arg) do
        %{id: __MODULE__, start: {__MODULE__, :start_link, [arg]}}
      end
    end
  end
end
```

**Wrong:**

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Worker do
  @moduledoc "A supervised worker base."

  defmacro __using__(_opts) do
    quote do
      @behaviour MyApp.Worker
      import MyApp.Worker.Internals

      def child_spec(arg) do
        %{id: __MODULE__, start: {__MODULE__, :start_link, [arg]}}
      end
    end
  end
end
```

**Why:** Some cases legitimately need injection: declaring a behaviour, defining `child_spec/1`, registering attributes (whether the macro is warranted at all is ADR-003). What the wrong version omits is any record of it. A developer reading `use MyApp.Worker` cannot see that a behaviour, a public `child_spec/1`, and an `import MyApp.Worker.Internals` were added without opening `__using__/1`. The `{: .info}` admonition is the documented contract for the names `use` injects into the caller. List only public-API additions: a private attribute such as `@_worker_meta` stays out of the label.

## Consequences

- Plain delegation uses lexically scoped `import`/`alias`; `use` is reserved for cases that genuinely require code injection.
- Name conflicts surface at the call site instead of being introduced by hidden propagated imports.
- The modules a file compile-depends on are visible in its directives rather than buried inside a `__using__/1` body (ADR-005).
- Where `use` remains, the moduledoc nutrition facts label documents exactly what it injects into the caller's public API.

description: When dispatching to modules whose names are built dynamically, write them as literal aliases or construct them inside a macro so the compiler tracks the compile-time dependency.
title: Untracked compile-time dependencies
body:
# ADR-005: Untracked compile-time dependencies

## Context

An Elixir alias such as `OtherModule.Foo` is just the atom `:"Elixir.OtherModule.Foo"`. When that alias appears literally in source, even outside any function and even inside a dynamic dispatch like `mod.example()`, the compiler records it in the calling module's compile-time dependency set. That set drives incremental compilation: when `OtherModule.Foo` changes, every module holding a compile-time dependency on it is recompiled.

This anti-pattern is the inverse of ADR-001 Compile-time dependencies. There the problem is too many tracked compile-time edges forcing wide recompilation; here the problem is an edge the compiler cannot see at all. It appears when a module name is built programmatically, either via `Module.concat/2` or by writing the underlying atom directly, instead of being written as a literal alias. The constructed name is identical at runtime, but the literal alias never enters the AST, so the dependency tracker never records it. The compiler sees a dependency only on the parent namespace `OtherModule`, never on `OtherModule.Foo` or `OtherModule.Bar`.

The failure is silent and surfaces as a stale build: editing `OtherModule.Foo` does not recompile the module that calls it, so the caller keeps invoking an outdated compiled version until a full rebuild. `mix xref trace path/to/file.ex` reports which modules a file depends on and whether each edge is compile-time, runtime, or export, and is the tool for confirming a dependency is actually tracked.

## Decision

### Rule 1: Reference modules by their literal alias

**Correct:**

```elixir
defmodule MyModule do
  mods = [OtherModule.Foo, OtherModule.Bar]

  for mod <- mods do
    mod.example()
  end
end
```

**Wrong:**

```elixir
defmodule MyModule do
  parts = [:Foo, :Bar]

  for part <- parts do
    Module.concat(OtherModule, part).example()
  end
end
```

**Why:** Even though the `for` dispatches dynamically, the literal aliases `OtherModule.Foo` and `OtherModule.Bar` appear in source outside any function, so the compiler records a compile-time dependency on each and recompiles `MyModule` when either changes. `Module.concat(OtherModule, part)` produces the same atom at runtime, but the compiler sees only `OtherModule`; the identical hole opens if you write the atom directly as `:"Elixir.OtherModule.Foo"`. A later edit to `OtherModule.Foo` then leaves `MyModule` compiled against a stale version with no recompilation triggered.

### Rule 2: When a name must be built dynamically, build it inside a macro

**Correct:**

```elixir
defmodule MyMacro do
  defmacro call_examples(parts) do
    for part <- parts do
      quote do
        # Builds the literal alias OtherModule.Foo at expansion time
        OtherModule.unquote(part).example()
      end
    end
  end
end

defmodule MyModule do
  import MyMacro
  call_examples([:Foo, :Bar])
end
```

**Wrong:**

```elixir
defmodule MyModule do
  parts = [:Foo, :Bar]

  for part <- parts do
    Module.concat(OtherModule, part).example()
  end
end
```

**Why:** `OtherModule.unquote(part)` is spliced during macro expansion, so the expanded AST of `MyModule` contains the literal aliases `OtherModule.Foo` and `OtherModule.Bar` before dependency tracking runs. The edges are recorded exactly as if the aliases had been typed by hand. `Module.concat/2` instead builds the atom at runtime, after dependency tracking has finished, so nothing is recorded. This is a legitimate use of a macro, the one job being to move name construction from runtime to compile time (ADR-003 covers when a macro is unnecessary).

## Consequences

- Editing any dispatched-to module recompiles its callers; incremental builds stay consistent and never call a stale compiled version.
- `mix xref trace` shows the intended compile-time edges to each concrete module instead of a single edge to the parent namespace.
- Dynamic dispatch over a known set of modules stays expressible, either as a literal alias list or via a compile-time macro, without sacrificing dependency tracking.
- The silent stale-build class of bug caused by runtime name construction is removed.
